selected_news.summary: Parts of the Canadian province of British Columbia may also be affected by the storms, which come as millions of people travel for the holiday.
selected_news.source_headline: California warns of flooding as King Tides peak over Thanksgiving
selected_news.article_text: Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said "Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too Storm Rachel batters Southern California, brings flooding to Las Vegas Storms targeting both US coasts threaten to snarl Thanksgiving travel for millions

selected_news.title: Kenneth Law, Kanadalı Zehir Satıcısı Özür Diledi
selected_news.summary: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, said he was remorseful for his actions.
selected_news.source_headline: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
selected_news.article_text: The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people" "What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said She also said Law's motives were financial "If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness "Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place." He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims "To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry." The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line 'Poison seller' who sold toxic chemicals online to people across world admits aiding suicides Man who sold toxic chemicals should rot in hell, says mother of woman who killed herself Survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair

selected_news.title: Oluwaseyi Dasho: Lagos'ta 7 milyon 2050'de sel riski
selected_news.summary: Cities including Lagos and Alexandria are sinking faster than previously thought, a new study shows.
selected_news.source_headline: New satellite data shows how fast some African cities are sinking
selected_news.article_text: Some of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure" This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated In the past, a lack of monitoring stations has prevented scientists from obtaining up-to-date localised information on subsidence in Africa, Dasho said But by using satellite data, the researchers from Virginia Tech were able to detect land movements as small as 1mm per year Senior author Manoochehr Shirzaei said Sentinel-1 satellites flew over the same region of the Earth every six to 12 days "[The satellite] transmits the radar signal, which hits the ground and bounces back to the satellite," the geosciences professor explained. This process is then repeated on "many revisits" The time between sending the signal and receiving it back is recorded, with changes in this value over time revealing how much the land has moved The ground under Alexandria and Lagos was found to have sunk an average of 6mm and 5mm per year respectively If this rate continued, sea levels around Alexandria would rise 36% more by 2050 than the IPCC predicted, external, under the middle estimates for how much planet-warming emissions will increase Luanda in Angola has also sunk significantly, but other cities such as Durban in South Africa have remained stable or even risen slightly Shirzaei said showing where the IPCC had underestimated risks - but also where the threat had been overestimated - could help planners allocate resources more effectively The man-made drivers of subsidence are usually "extremely local, [which] means that we can combat them by creating local policies", Shirzaei explained One major cause is the increased water consumption of rapidly growing cities. Too much water being extracted from the ground can lead to the soil becoming compacted and the surface sinking The Aswan Dam on the Nile may also be trapping sediment upstream and preventing the replacement of sinking land in Alexandria, the study suggests In Lagos, the reclaiming of land from the ocean to create artificial islands and the construction of buildings on loose ground are other possible causes of subsidence Why are some cities sinking? Hear from those trying to solve the problem Methods of preventing cities from sinking include supplying other water sources and growing less water-intensive crops "Whatever we cannot mitigate, we try to adapt to it," Shirzaei added. This could mean building flood defences or moving key infrastructure to a higher level The professor said developing countries had been "left out" of much of the planning for sea-level rises due to a lack of monitoring The techniques developed in this study could potentially be used to address the knowledge gap in other regions, such as the Pacific islands, Shirzaei suggested Oluwaseyi Dasho said he hoped the paper, in Science Advances,, external could help African governments "prepare adequately for future challenges and more importantly for the future generations" More climate money for Africa? selected_news.source_headline: After Antalya: Climate Diplomacy’s Crisis of Trust
selected_news.article_text: The most revealing outcome of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya was not simply the failure to agree on its central political package. It was the growing difficulty of sustaining a shared climate agenda when governments remain divided over who should bear the costs of change, how quickly that change should happen, and what support developing countries can realistically expect At the closing plenary on November 22, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell acknowledged that agreement had not been reached on the presidency-led decisions. He also pointed to decisions adopted elsewhere in the negotiations, including on a just transition. Antalya therefore ended neither with a comprehensive political settlement nor with the complete absence of progress. Its outcome was more uncomfortable: parts of the process moved forward, but the political understanding needed to hold them together remained out of reach For international development, this distinction matters. Climate negotiations are not only about emissions targets or the wording of diplomatic texts. They are also negotiations over investment, livelihoods, public finances and the distribution of economic opportunity. When these dimensions are treated as separate concerns, governments may agree on individual measures while remaining unable to agree on the broader direction Claims that COP31 achieved “nothing” overlook the decisions that were adopted. The UN climate secretariat’s official outcomes page lists decisions covering issues including just transition, the global goal on adaptation, long-term climate finance, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, technology transfer and capacity-building. Their adoption, however, does not by itself establish that the resulting provisions are sufficiently ambitious or adequately funded. That requires scrutiny of the individual texts. The opposite interpretation is equally misleading. Technical decisions and implementation initiatives cannot fully compensate for the absence of political agreement on the questions dividing governments The distinction is practical, not semantic. A decision may keep an institution functioning or advance a particular negotiating track without resolving the wider dispute over responsibility and resources. Governments can continue producing outcomes while losing confidence in the bargain that underpins them. Antalya’s central problem was therefore not a complete lack of activity. It was the failure to bring that activity into a credible common framework The dispute over fossil fuels raises a question that cannot be settled through diplomatic language alone: what would it mean, in practice, to implement a transition away from them? Speaking in Antalya on 13 November, UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for an accelerated transition that is just, orderly and equitable. He linked the expansion of clean power, grids, storage and energy efficiency to reductions in fossil-fuel production, consumption and emissions. That connection is essential. Announcing more clean-energy investment does not, on its own, establish how dependence on high-emitting energy sources will decline. A credible transition needs evidence of change across the energy system, rather than a growing list of projects presented without reference to their wider effect Yet credibility also requires attention to national circumstances. The pace and design of transition cannot be identical everywhere. Governments face different fiscal constraints, institutional capacities and development priorities The task is to reconcile a clear global direction with workable national pathways. Flexibility should help countries implement the transition, not provide an indefinite exemption from it. Equally, greater ambition should come with a serious account of how countries with fewer resources will finance the changes expected of them For developing countries, climate finance is not an additional benefit to be negotiated after the main agreement. It is part of what makes an agreement deliverable An official COP31 discussion on implementation highlighted calls for more accessible finance, stronger technical assistance and closer international cooperation to help developing countries turn their climate plans into action. Participants also stressed the need to account for differing national circumstances and capacities. This points to a weakness in the way progress is often assessed. The headline value of a financial pledge says little about when money will become available, how difficult it will be to access, or whether national institutions can use it effectively. A more useful assessment would ask whether funding reaches an implementable project, whether its terms are appropriate, and whether the receiving country has the capacity to sustain the investment The gap is particularly stark in adaptation. In Antalya, Guterres warned that even tripling adaptation finance would cover less than 30% of estimated needs. The relevant comparison, then, is not only with previous pledges. It is with the scale of the risks countries are being asked to manage. From a development perspective, adaptation should be treated as an investment in the continuity of essential services, livelihoods and economic activity. Leaving it underfunded weakens the foundations on which wider development plans depend Electrification featured prominently in the implementation agenda. In his closing remarks, Stiell pointed to national commitments and leaders’ announcements indicating momentum across economies representing roughly half of the global economy. He also highlighted the Electrification Implementation Package as evidence that practical work was continuing alongside the negotiations Such initiatives deserve attention, but their status and purpose must remain clear. An implementation initiative is not the same as a universally agreed negotiating outcome. Nor does increased electricity use automatically demonstrate a successful climate transition. Guterres’s remarks in Antalya stressed clean electrification alongside an actual reduction in fossil-fuel dependence and emissions. There is also a development test that should not be lost in the discussion of investment totals and deployment targets Will electrification improve the reliability of essential services? Will households and smaller businesses be able to afford it? Will investment strengthen local skills and institutions, or leave countries dependent on capabilities they cannot maintain? These questions belong at the centre of implementation. Public confidence will be difficult to sustain if the transition is visible in international announcements but not in the quality or affordability of everyday services Here is a list of articles selected by our Editorial Board that have gained significant interest from the public For Arab countries, the lesson should not be reduced to a choice between defending existing energy interests and accepting an externally defined transition. A stronger approach would connect climate negotiations to a broader development agenda. That means placing adaptation finance, water and food security, economic diversification, technology access and workforce development within the same policy conversation. It also requires acknowledging that Arab countries do not have identical interests or capacities. A useful common position should accommodate those differences rather than conceal them behind a single defensive message The objective should be to secure the conditions for a manageable transition: credible support, realistic implementation pathways and protection for people whose livelihoods may be affected. At the same time, regional diplomacy should contribute practical proposals rather than focus primarily on resisting unwelcome language.The strength of a negotiating position lies partly in what it can prevent. Its longer-term value lies in what it can help deliver Antalya will inevitably renew calls to reform the COP process. Stiell himself acknowledged the need to improve and modernise it, stressing transparency, participation and consensus-building as the process moves further into implementation. There is a legitimate debate about whether the current format makes the best use of political attention and negotiating capacity. But changing how often conferences take place would not, by itself, resolve disagreements over finance, fossil fuels or responsibility.The more important questions concern how decisions are prepared and followed through. Are major disputes addressed early enough, or repeatedly deferred to the final hours? Do commitments identify who is responsible for delivery? Are resources and timelines attached? Can governments and the public distinguish between an announcement, an adopted decision and a funded programme? Reform should make those distinctions clearer. It should also preserve meaningful participation by countries with smaller delegations and by communities most exposed to climate risks. A more efficient process would be of limited value if it became less representative Stiell described COP32 as a critical milestone and stressed that the second global stocktake must build on the first rather than retreat from it. That sets a political expectation for the next conference. It does not, in itself, establish that every unresolved issue from Antalya has been formally transferred into a single negotiating package. The immediate challenge is to prevent political disappointment from becoming an excuse for delay. Confidence can begin to recover before the next summit through results that can be checked: finance reaching intended recipients, adaptation programmes moving into implementation, measurable emissions reductions, and support reaching workers and communities affected by economic change. Antalya exposed the limits of a process that can sustain considerable activity without securing agreement on its collective direction. The response should be neither to dismiss multilateral negotiations nor to excuse their shortcomings COP32 will need a stronger political settlement. But its credibility will depend on something less easily negotiated in a closing plenary: evidence that existing commitments are improving people’s prospects, reducing their exposure to risk and making development more secure Editor’s Note: The opinions expressed here by the authors are their own, not those of Impakter.com

selected_news.quality_narration: Antalya’da gerçekleşen COP31 iklim zirvesi, ortak bir siyasi paket oluşturulamasa da adil geçiş ve kayıp‑zarar fonu gibi kararlar alındı. Birleşmiş Milletler İklim Değişikliği Yürütme Sekreteri Simon Stiell, COP32’nin daha güçlü bir siyasi uzlaşı gerektirdiğini vurguladı. Uzmanlar, gelecekteki başarının finansmanın hedeflenen alıcılara ulaşması ve adaptasyon projelerinin hayata geçirilmesiyle ölçüleceğini belirtiyor.
